name: FHFA on AI in Housing Finance: Use Case Inventories, Compliance Plans and a TechSprint
title: FHFA on AI in Housing Finance: Use Case Inventories, Compliance Plans and a TechSprint
answer: The Federal Housing Finance Agency publishes its annual AI use case inventories, AI compliance plans and news of its Generative AI in Housing Finance TechSprint. The inventories are the most concrete material, listing named AI systems such as a generative AI legal research tool and neural networks applied to loan-level mortgage data, with fields covering training data, human oversight and disparity mitigation. Together they show how the regulator of Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and the Federal Home Loan Banks documents and governs its own use of AI.

sections.body: The Federal Housing Finance Agency, which regulates Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and the 11 Federal Home Loan Banks, publishes these pages on fhfa.gov. They comprise the 2024 and 2025 AI use case inventories, issued as CSV files under the title 2024 Federal Housing Finance Agency AI Reporting per EO 14110, the 2024 and 2025 AI Compliance Plans, and a news release on the 2024 Generative AI in Housing Finance TechSprint. The compliance plans state they satisfy requirements of OMB Memoranda M-24-10 and M-25-21 and Section 104(c) of the AI in Government Act of 2020.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The inventories are structured reporting templates. Section 1 covers use case identifiers, agency and bureau, topic area and whether the use case appears in a list of general commercial AI products. Section 2 covers intended purpose and expected benefits, system outputs, whether a use case should be withheld from public reporting, stage of development, and whether it is rights-impacting, safety-impacting, both or neither. Section 3 covers agency-owned training, fine-tuning and evaluation data, documentation, demographic variables used as model features, custom code and open-source links. Section 4 covers Authority to Operate, system name, developer tool wait times, centralized IT provisioning and computing resource requests. Section 5 covers AI impact assessments, independent evaluations, post-deployment monitoring, human oversight, notice of AI use, and steps to detect and mitigate disparities. The 2025 file names specific systems. LexisNexis, coded FHFA-1 under the Office of General Counsel, is a deployed generative AI legal research tool that searches for and summarizes legal information, operational since 1 October 2023, vendor-purchased and without an Authority to Operate. Neural Networks for the FHFA Modeling Analytics Platform, coded FHFA-2 under DHMG, is deployed classical predictive machine learning, operational since 5 January 2024, developed in-house, using borrower-level monthly mortgage data and income as a demographic feature, with custom code, to identify nonlinearities, anomalies and important variables and improve Single-Family platform forecasts. A third entry covers phishing email identification. The TechSprint news release describes a three-day in-person event from 22 July 2024 in Washington, D.C., run by the Office of Financial Technology, asking how responsible generative AI might promote a transparent, fair, equitable and inclusive housing finance system, with a Demo Day on 25 July and applications due 24 May 2024.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source states that FHFA regulates Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and the 11 Federal Home Loan Banks, which provide more than $8.4 trillion in funding for U.S. mortgage markets and financial institutions. It dates the Fintech Office launch to July 2022. It records operational dates of 1 October 2023 for the LexisNexis legal research tool and 5 January 2024 for the neural network modeling use case, and notes that the former has no Authority to Operate. It states that the compliance plans satisfy Section 3(a)(iii) of M-24-10 and Section 3(b)(ii) of M-25-21, and Section 104(c) of the AI in Government Act of 2020.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in real estate gets the regulator's own account of how it governs AI, including the fields it uses to test for rights and safety impacts, demographic variables in models, human oversight and disparity mitigation. The named use cases show generative AI entering legal and administrative work and classical machine learning applied to loan-level mortgage data, which is the analytical layer behind housing finance decisions. The TechSprint shows where the agency is pushing industry experimentation on responsible generative AI.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Real Estate

sections.body: These pages cover FHFA's internal AI governance and its convening role, not the automated valuation model rulemaking or supervisory expectations for regulated entities. The inventories are template-driven and largely empty of results beyond the named use cases, and the compliance plans are statements of alignment with OMB memoranda rather than detailed operational guidance. The TechSprint material is a single 2024 event announcement, and the pages carry no independent evaluation data.
